text: Then a great outcry arose from the people and their wives against their fellow Jews.
Some were saying, "With our sons and daughters we are many; we must get grain so we can eat and stay alive."

versions.text: Some were saying, "We have many sons and daughters. To get grain, we have to eat and stay alive."
versions.explanation: The purpose clause is reversed. The Hebrew says "let us get grain that we may eat and live" — grain is the means, eating and living the goal. As rendered, "To get grain, we have to eat and stay alive" is illogical and obscures the complaint about hunger.

text: Others were saying, "We are mortgaging our fields, our vineyards, and our houses to get grain during the famine."
And still others were saying, "We have borrowed money against our fields and vineyards to pay the king's tax.

Now our flesh is the same as the flesh of our brothers, our children the same as theirs, yet here we are forcing our sons and daughters into slavery. Some of our daughters have already been enslaved, and we are powerless to act, for our fields and vineyards belong to others.

versions.text: Now our flesh is the same as the flesh of our brothers, our children the same as theirs, yet here we are forcing our sons and daughters into slavery. Some of our daughters have already been taken, and we are powerless, because our fields and vineyards belong to others."
versions.explanation: The Hebrew simply joins the clauses; "because" imposes a causal link that reverses the logic (loss of land is the result of their helplessness, not its cause). "Powerless to act" better renders אֵין לְאֵל יָדֵנוּ, and "enslaved" matches נִכְבָּשׁוֹת more closely than the vague "taken."

text: When I heard their outcry and these complaints, I was furious.

versions.text: When I heard their outcry and these charges, I was furious.
versions.explanation: הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה refers to the words/complaints the people had just voiced, not to formal accusations. "Charges" also collides with the legal sense of "brought charges" in the next verse, blurring who is accusing whom.

text: After thinking it over, I brought charges against the nobles and officials. I told them, "You are exacting interest from your own brothers!" And I called a great assembly to deal with them.

I said to them, "As far as we were able, we have bought back our fellow Jews who had been sold to the nations. And now you are selling your own brothers, only for them to be sold back to us!" They said nothing, for they could find no answer.
So I continued, "What you are doing is not right. Should you not walk in the fear of our God to avoid the taunts of the nations, our enemies?
I myself, along with my brothers and my men, have been lending the people money and grain. Let us stop charging interest!

Give back to them this very day their fields, their vineyards, their olive groves, and their houses, and also the hundredth part of the money, the grain, the new wine, and the oil that you have exacted from them."

versions.text: Give back to them this very day their fields, their vineyards, their olive groves, and their houses, along with the interest you have exacted from them—the hundredth part of the money, the grain, the new wine, and the oil."
versions.explanation: The interpretive insertion "the interest" followed by an em-dash gloss makes the sentence hard to follow when read aloud, and doubles the same idea. A single clause following the Hebrew word order reads more smoothly and stays closer to the text.

text: They answered, "We will give it back, and we will demand nothing more from them. We will do just as you say." Then I summoned the priests and made them take an oath to keep this promise.

I also shook out the fold of my robe and said, "So may God shake out of his house and his property every man who does not keep this promise. May he be shaken out and left empty!" The whole assembly said, "Amen," and praised the LORD. And the people did as they had promised.

Moreover, from the day I was appointed governor in the land of Judah—from the twentieth year until the thirty-second year of King Artaxerxes, twelve years in all—neither I nor my brothers ate the food allotted to the governor.

The earlier governors, my predecessors, had laid a heavy burden on the people, taking food and wine from them, besides forty shekels of silver. Their assistants also lorded it over the people. But I did not act that way, because I feared God.

versions.text: The earlier governors, my predecessors, had laid a heavy burden on the people, taking forty shekels of silver from them along with food and wine. Their assistants also lorded it over the people. But I did not act that way, because I feared God.
versions.explanation: The Hebrew lists food and wine as the primary exaction, with the forty shekels of silver as an additional charge (אַחַר, "besides"). The current wording makes the silver primary and loses the sense of "in addition."

text: What is more, I devoted myself to the work on this wall. We bought no land, and all my men were gathered there for the work.

versions.text: Instead, I devoted myself to the work on this wall. We bought no land, and all my men were assigned to the work.
versions.explanation: וְגַם is additive ("moreover, what is more"), not adversative; "Instead" turns the clause into a contrast the Hebrew does not signal. Also, קְבוּצִים שָׁם ("gathered there") locates the men at the wall, which "assigned to the work" loses.

text: Furthermore, a hundred and fifty Jews and officials ate at my table, along with those who came to us from the surrounding nations.

Each day one ox, six choice sheep, and poultry were prepared for me, and every ten days an abundant supply of wine. Yet in spite of all this, I never demanded the food allotted to the governor, because the burden on this people was heavy.
Remember me with favor, my God, for all I have done for this people.
